chapter: History IV · The Age of Industrialisation
source: NCERT India and the Contemporary World II (Class X History), Chapter IV

overview.bigIdea: Pictures of 1900 showed industrialisation as magic progress. The real history is slower and wider: **proto-industry before factories**, **hand labour alongside steam**, and in India a colony where **weavers declined, then survived**, while factories grew under colonial limits.

ladder.a: Slow; cotton then iron; hand labour preferred
China traders, Tatas, jobbers; small-scale still dominant; adverts

languages.name: Both sides
languages.text: Factories AND workshops; decline AND survival of weavers.

languages.name: Sources
languages.text: Read the magistrate, Patna and millworker sources.

plan.text: Lessons 1–2 – proto-industrialisation, factory, pace of change, hand labour.
Lesson 3 – Company control and Manchester (data activity).
Lessons 4–5 – entrepreneurs, workers, war, small-scale industry, advertisements.
Check knowledge quiz; revise after 1, 3 and 7 days.

lessons.title: Before the Industrial Revolution
lessons.hook: Long before factory chimneys, English cloth was made in **village homes**. A merchant clothier moved wool from stapler to spinner to weaver to fuller to dyer – controlling hundreds of workers without a single factory.

core.def: Large-scale industrial production for an international market, not based on factories, before the factory age.
Town guilds controlled production and blocked newcomers; enclosures pushed cottagers and poor peasants to seek extra income.
Merchants in towns, work in villages; finishing in London; 20–25 workers per stage per merchant.
Earliest English factories by the 1730s; cotton imports 2.5 million lb (1760) → 22 million lb (1787); Arkwright’s cotton mill brought processes under one roof.

explain: **For peasant households:** income from proto-industry supplemented shrinking farm income and allowed fuller use of family labour.
**For mill owners:** supervision, quality control and regulation of labour became possible under one roof.

example.q: Explain what is meant by proto-industrialisation. (3 marks)
steps: **Meaning:** the phase of large-scale industrial production for an international market before factories, based in rural households.
**How it worked:** merchants from towns gave advances to peasants and artisans to produce for them; guilds made town production difficult.
**Network:** controlled by merchants – wool stapler → spinners → weavers → fullers → dyers, finished in London; goods made within family farms.

lessons.tip: ‘Why did merchants turn to the countryside?’ = guilds in towns (push) + enclosures and poor peasants needing income (pull).
lessons.memory: Proto = early · Guilds block towns · Stapler → spinner → weaver → fuller → dyer → London · 1730s factories · 2.5 → 22 million lb.

lessons.title: The pace of change, hand labour and workers’ lives
lessons.hook: James Watt’s improved steam engine was patented in **1781** – yet by 1800 all of England had only **321** steam engines. Why were factory owners so slow to use the ‘magic’ machine?

core.def: Cotton up to the 1840s, then iron and steel (railways); by 1873 iron and steel exports £77 million, double cotton.
Less than 20% of workforce in advanced sectors by 1900; new technology expensive, broke down, repair costly, not as effective as claimed.
Plentiful cheap labour; seasonal demand (gas works, breweries, printers, ships); 500 kinds of hammers, 45 kinds of axes; upper classes liked hand-made goods.
Jobs via friends and kin; nights under bridges, Night Refuges, Casual Wards; seasonal unemployment; 10% extremely poor; 35–75% unemployed in 1830s slumps.
James Hargreaves, 1764; one wheel, many spindles; women hand spinners attacked it.

explain: **America vs Britain:** with labour shortage, America mechanised; Britain had no problem hiring hands.
**After the 1840s:** building boom – roads, stations, tunnels, sewers; transport workers doubled in the 1840s and again in 30 years.

example.q: Why did some industrialists in 19th-century Europe prefer hand labour over machines? (5 marks)
steps: **Cheap labour:** poor peasants and vagrants flooded the cities; wages were low.
**Costly machines:** required large capital, broke down, repair was costly.
**Seasonal demand:** gas works, breweries, printers needed extra hands only in some seasons.
**Variety:** demand was for intricate designs – 500 varieties of hammers, 45 kinds of axes needed skill.
**Taste:** the upper classes preferred hand-made goods as a symbol of refinement; machine goods went to the colonies.

mistakes: Saying most British workers were machine operators by 1900.
Forgetting women hand spinners were the ones who attacked the Jenny.
lessons.tip: Learn three numbers that prove slow change: 321 engines, under 20% of workforce, typical worker = craftsperson.
lessons.memory: Watt 1781 · 321 engines · £77m iron · <20% · Jenny 1764 (Hargreaves) · 500 hammers, 45 axes.

lessons.title: Indian textiles, weavers and Manchester
lessons.hook: In 1772 a Company official boasted that no nation could match Indian textiles. Within 80 years, piece-goods fell from a third of India’s exports to **3 per cent** – and Manchester cloth flooded Indian bazaars.

core.def: Fine cottons and silks dominated world markets; land route via the north-west to Afghanistan, Persia, Central Asia; ports Surat, Masulipatam, Hoogly.
European companies got concessions and monopolies; Surat Rs 16 million → Rs 3 million by the 1740s; Bombay and Calcutta grew.
After 1760s: eliminated traders and brokers; gomasthas; advances tied weavers; no selling to others; low prices; floggings.
Import duties in Britain; British goods pushed into India; piece-goods 33% of exports (1811–12) → 3% (1850–51); cotton goods 31% of imports (1850) → over 50% (1870s).
American Civil War (1860s): raw cotton exported to Britain, prices shot up; then Indian factories competed too.

explain: **Weavers’ response:** deserted villages, revolted with village traders, refused loans, closed workshops, became agricultural labourers.
**Two problems at once:** export market collapsed and the local market was glutted with cheap machine-made imports.

example.q: How did the East India Company procure regular supplies of cotton and silk textiles from Indian weavers? (5 marks)
steps: **Political power:** after the 1760s in Bengal and Carnatic it asserted a monopoly right to trade.
**Removing middlemen:** existing traders and brokers were eliminated for direct control.
**Gomasthas:** paid servants supervised weavers, collected supplies and checked quality.
**Advances:** loans for raw material bound weavers to hand cloth only to the gomastha.
**Control by force:** gomasthas came with sepoys and peons, punished delays; prices stayed low.
example.answer: Monopoly → no brokers → gomasthas → advances → coercion.

mistakes: Saying textile exports fell immediately after 1760 (they did not at first).
Saying the American Civil War helped Indian weavers.
lessons.tip: Manchester answers: two numbers for exports (33% → 3%) and two for imports (31% → 50%).
lessons.memory: Surat Rs 16m → 3m · Gomastha · 1811–12: 33% → 1850–51: 3% · Imports 31% → 50% · Civil War = cotton shortage.

lessons.title: Factories come up; peculiarities of industrial growth
lessons.hook: The first Bombay cotton mill came up in **1854**. Its capital came from opium and tea traders, its workers from Ratnagiri villages – and they still went home every harvest.

core.def: Bombay cotton mill 1854 (4 mills by 1862); Bengal jute 1855 and 1862; Elgin Mill, Kanpur 1860s; Ahmedabad a year later; Madras 1874.
China trade: Dwarkanath Tagore (six joint-stock companies, 1830s–40s), Dinshaw Petit, J.N. Tata, Seth Hukumchand (jute, 1917), Birla’s family; others traded with Burma, Middle East, East Africa.
Barred from trading manufactures with Europe; edged out of shipping; European Managing Agencies – Bird Heiglers, Andrew Yule, Jardine Skinner – controlled industry; separate chambers of commerce.
584,000 (1901) → over 2,436,000 (1946); from nearby districts (Ratnagiri for Bombay); jobbers recruited and controlled.
Coarse yarn first; swadeshi and loss of China market → cloth (doubled 1900–1912); First World War boom; Manchester never recovered.
67% of large industries in Bengal and Bombay (1911); factories had 5% (1911) and 10% (1931) of industrial labour; handloom output almost trebled 1900–1940; fly shuttles 35% by 1941.

explain: **Managing Agencies** invested in tea, coffee, mining, indigo and jute – mostly for export, not for sale in India.
**Weavers survived** by new technology (fly shuttle) and specialised fine weaves – but lived hard lives with the whole household working.

example.q: Why did industrial production in India increase during the First World War? (3/5 marks)
steps: **Fewer imports:** British mills were busy with war production, so Manchester imports declined.
**Home market:** Indian mills suddenly had a vast home market to supply.
**War orders:** jute bags, cloth for army uniforms, tents, leather boots, horse and mule saddles.
**Expansion:** new factories set up, old ones ran multiple shifts, more workers worked longer hours.
**After the war:** Manchester never recaptured its position; local industrialists captured the home market.
example.answer: Imports fell + home market + war orders = boom.

mistakes: Saying Indian mills first made fine cloth (they made coarse yarn).
Saying factories employed most industrial workers (5–10%).
Confusing the jobber with the gomastha.
lessons.tip: ‘Who set up industries?’ – China traders (Tagore, Petit, Tata, Hukumchand), internal traders, and the limits set by Managing Agencies.
lessons.memory: 1854 Bombay · 1855 jute · 1912 Tata steel · 1917 Hukumchand · Jobber · 5% → 10% · Handloom ×3 · Fly shuttle 35%.

lessons.title: Market for goods
lessons.hook: Lakshmi on a cloth bundle, Vishnu bringing sunlight for a soap, baby Krishna selling gripe water – early advertisers in India knew exactly how to make foreign goods feel familiar.

core.def: ‘MADE IN MANCHESTER’ as a mark of quality; images of gods (Kartika, Lakshmi, Saraswati) gave divine approval; historic figures like Maharaja Ranjit Singh created respect.
Seen by people who could not read; hung in tea shops, homes and offices all year.
If you respect the king or nawab, respect the product.
Indian manufacturers: if you care for the nation, buy what Indians produce.

explain: **Conclusion of the chapter:** industrialisation meant technological change, factories and a new workforce – but hand technology and small-scale production remained important. The ‘magic’ images of 1900 tell only part of the story.

example.q: How did advertisements help expand markets for new products in India? (3 marks)
steps: **Labels:** ‘Made in Manchester’ built trust; images of Indian gods made foreign goods familiar and gave divine approval.
**Calendars:** reached even people who could not read, seen daily in tea shops and homes.
**Swadeshi:** Indian manufacturers used adverts to carry the nationalist message – buy Indian.
example.answer: Labels, calendars, royal and religious images, swadeshi message.

mistakes: Saying only Indian manufacturers used gods’ images (Manchester labels did too).
lessons.tip: Link this to Chapter II: Swaraj and swadeshi – advertisements carried the nationalist message.
lessons.memory: Made in Manchester · Gods = approval + familiarity · Calendars for all · Kings = quality · Swadeshi adverts.
examAsk: How did manufacturers use advertisements to sell goods in India?
What message did Indian manufacturers’ advertisements carry?

cards.a: Divine approval; foreign goods seem familiar.
Seen daily, even by people who could not read.
Swadeshi – buy Indian for the nation.

revision: Images like ‘Dawn of the Century’ and ‘Two Magicians’ glorified machines; the real story was slower.
Proto-industrialisation: merchants gave advances to rural households; guilds blocked towns; London as finishing centre.
Factories in England by the 1730s; cotton imports 2.5 → 22 million lb (1760–1787); Arkwright’s mill.
Cotton led till the 1840s, then iron and steel (£77 million by 1873).
Slow change: under 20% in advanced sectors; 321 steam engines; typical worker a craftsperson.
Hand labour preferred: cheap plentiful labour, seasonal demand, variety of designs, upper-class taste.
Workers: jobs via kin; seasonal unemployment; 35–75% unemployed in the 1830s; women attacked the Spinning Jenny (1764).
India dominated fine textiles; Surat and Hoogly declined (Rs 16m → 3m), Bombay and Calcutta grew.
Company control: gomasthas, advances, no other buyers, low prices; weavers deserted, revolted or quit.
Manchester: piece-goods 33% → 3% of exports; cotton goods 31% → over 50% of imports; American Civil War raised cotton prices.
First mills: Bombay 1854, jute 1855, Madras 1874; Tata steel 1912; Hukumchand jute 1917.
Capital from China trade; European Managing Agencies controlled industry; jobbers recruited workers.
Coarse yarn first; shift to cloth after 1906; First World War boom.
Small-scale dominated: factories 5% (1911), 10% (1931); handloom almost trebled 1900–40; fly shuttle.
Advertising: Manchester labels, gods, calendars, kings; Indian swadeshi adverts.

sections.title: Britain vs India answers · 4 steps
items: Say which country and period you are describing.
Give the main change with one figure.
Add the human side (workers, weavers).
End with the ‘peculiarity’ – slow change or survival of small-scale work.

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line introduction using the textbook’s key term (e.g. ‘Proto-industrialisation was …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, key term first. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a date, a name or a figure from the chapter to each point – but only when you are sure of it.
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Compare’ draw a small two-column table.
Source-based questions: underline the key line in the source first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn timelines and sorts – if you get every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can explain proto-industrialisation and why merchants went to villages.
I can explain why industrial change in Britain was slow and why hand labour was preferred.
I can describe workers’ lives and opposition to the Spinning Jenny.
I can explain how the Company controlled weavers and how Manchester affected them.
I can describe early Indian entrepreneurs, workers and the war-time growth.
I can explain why small-scale industry survived and how goods were advertised.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark source-based and 5-mark long answers; History also has map work). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
